topic_info.title: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (diastolic heart failure)

author.author_institution: John Peter Smith Family Medicine Residency

editor.editor_institution: Augusta University − University of Georgia Medical Partnership

list.listitem: Patients with diastolic heart failure (also called heart failure with preserved ejection fraction or HFpEF) have typical signs and symptoms of heart failure (exertional dyspnea, fatigue, pulmonary or peripheral fluid accumulation) but left ventricular ejection fraction is relatively preserved. C

The most common cause of diastolic heart failure is hypertensive heart disease. Apart from the treatment of hypertension, pharmacotherapy shown to reduce mortality or improve symptoms in systolic heart failure (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction or HFrEF) has not been shown to reduce mortality in HFpEF. Some of these agents may cause harm. B

HFpEF is a syndrome of preserved ejection fraction (>40%) with impaired diastolic function (increased cardiac stiffness, impaired relaxation, and elevated filling pressures) with clinical signs and symptoms of heart failure (edema, shortness of breath, exertional dyspnea).
HFpEF and HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction) each comprise approximately 50% of cases of heart failure.
Diastolic heart failure is more prevalent in the elderly, in women, and in patients with hypertension.
The gender ratio of patients with diastolic heart failure is reversed from that of systolic heart failure; approximately 70% of patients with diastolic heart failure are women.
Hypertensive heart disease
Valvular disease (i.e mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis).
Right ventricular dysfunction secondary to pulmonary hypertension, pulmonary thromboembolic disorders, or intrinsic lung disease.
Pericardial disease (constrictive pericarditis).
Ischemic heart disease is a less common cause of HFpEF than HFrEF.
One proposed mechanism of diastolic heart failure is impaired filling during diastole.
This may be due to hypertrophy, increased extracellular matrix, abnormal calcium handling causing delayed relaxation, or increased arterial stiffness.
The term "diastolic heart failure" is likely to cover a number of pathophysiological mechanisms.
Abnormal coupling of ventricular function to a "stiff" vascular system is thought to contribute.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Valvular disease, especially aortic or mitral stenosis

list.listitem: Symptoms and signs do not reliably distinguish between systolic heart failure and diastolic heart failure. C

The diagnosis of HFpEF is made on the basis of imaging results showing preserved systolic function (primarily by echocardiogram) and diastolic dysfunction in the presence of the clinical signs and symptoms of heart failure. C

The 2016 European Society of Cardiology guidelines define heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) as: A preserved EF (>50%) with objective echocardiographic evidence of impaired diastolic function (patients with EF 40% to 49% are classified as heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction or HFmrEF). Elevated levels of BNP (>35 pg/mL) or NT-proBNP (>125 pg/mL) and at least one additional criterion: a) relevant structural heart disease such as LVH and/or left atrial enlargment or b) diastolic dysfunction. Clinical signs and symptoms of heart failure.
The definition for heart failure with mildly reduced ejection fraction (also called mid-range ejection fraction) or HFmrEF is the same, other than an ejection fraction between 40% and 49%.

The American Society for Echocardiography (2016 Guideline) recommends the use of a combination of echocardiographic findings to support a diagnosis of diastolic dysfunction and reccommends that all echocardiogram reports comment on diastolic function.

The symptoms and signs of heart failure do not distinguish between systolic and diastolic heart failure. In one cross-sectional study, standard clinical criteria for heart failure were similarly accurate for systolic and diastolic heart failure. The absence of a S3 gallop or a displaced point-of-maximal impuse (PMI) is not specific for HFpEF.

The diagnosis is made on the basis of the clinical symptoms and signs of heart failure with preserved LVEF on echocardiography or other form of imaging. See "Diagnostic Criteria" above for a full definition.
The diagnostic accuracy of the symptoms and signs of heart failure (using both definitions) are shown in the chapter on systolic heart failure.
Clinical prediction rules are only moderately accurate for diagnosing heart failure in patients presenting with dyspnea.

Echocardiogram may demonstrate abnormal filling patterns or pressures, increased left ventricular wall thickness, or an enlarged left atrium. A cominbation of these markers is used to support a diagnosis of diastolic dysfunction. Echocardiogram can also provide evidence for other causes of HFpEF (infiltrative cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis, valvular disease).

B-natriuretic peptide reflects tension in the myocardium and therefore detects both systolic and diastolic dysfunction. BNP values <35 pg/mL or NT-proBNP values <125 pg/mL in ambulatory patients have high negative predictive values. European guidelines suggest using BNP levels above these thresholds to decide who merits further diagnostic imaging. Optimal BNP cut-offs are a topic of ongoing study although 35 pg/ml for BNP and 125 pg/ml for NT-proBNP are widely used.
Patients presenting with heart failure with preserved systolic function should be evaluated for the presence of ischemic heart disease, although ischemic testing is not always indicated.

A simple clinical prediction rule using noninvasive data can identify patients at low, moderate, and high risk for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). The independent predictors were BMI > 30 kg/m2 (2 points), taking 2 or more antihypertensive drugs (1 point), afib (3 points), Doppler echo with pulmonary artery systolic pressure greater than 35 mm Hg, age 60 years or older, and Doppler echo showing an E/e ratio of more than 9. The authors suggest that the diagnosis can be provisionally ruled out for patients with 0 or 1 points, ruled in for patients with more than 5 points, and that further testing is needed for those with 2 to 5 points.Although validated in a separate group of patients, the validation group was from the same center, so prospective validation should still be performed in a separate population by another group of investigators.
Guideline-based screening for and treatment of cardiovascular risk factors and conditions which often co-exist with HFpEF (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, diabetes mellitus, atrial fibrillation).
Symptomatic relief of edema with diuretics.
Exclusion of other causes of HFpEF, including valvular heart disease, constrictive pericarditis, and infiltrative cardiomyopathy.
Patients with HFpEF and symptoms of volume overload should be treated with diuretics. A
Guideline-based treatment of co-exisiting cardiovascular risk factors (atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia) does not differ in patients with HFpEF. C
There is limited evidence to support any specific medication to reduce symptoms (other than diuretics), cardiovascular mortality, or all-cause mortality. A
Sodium glucose cotransporter inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and angiotensin receptor blockers may reduce HFpEF-related hospitalizations. B
Ambulatory patients should exercise, control BP to target, and limit salt. B
Emphasis should be placed on reaching guideline-directed blood pressure target, following a low-sodium diet, and controlling the ventricular rate for patients with atrial fibrillation..

A 2018 Cochrane Review concluded that mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRA) may reduce HFpEF-related hospitalizations. Angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB), and beta blockers (BB) have not been shown to reduce morbidity or mortality in HFpEF when not indicated for another reason.

Spironolactone appears to be associated with a decrease in heart failure-specific hospitalizations, though not in all-cause hospitalizations or CV and all-cause mortality. Additionally, spironolactone does not appear to improve clinical symptoms, and may decrease exercise capacity as compared to placebo.
A meta-analysis found reduction in all cause and cardiovascular mortality for heart failure patients treated with SGLT2 inhibitors.

A trial of Candesartan in 3,023 patients with NYHA class II-IV heart failure and preserved EF showed a modest reduction in hospitalizations related to heart failure, though no difference in mortality or all-cause hospitalizations as compared to placebo. A separate trial, comparing Irbesartan to placebo in 4,128 patients with symptomatic HFpEF, showed no difference between groups with regards to either hospitalizations or mortality.

Nebivolol does not appear to reduce all-cause hospitalization or mortality, or combined all-cause mortality and CV hospitalization, as compared to placebo in patients over age 70 with symptomatic HF and EF >35%.A smaller study studying Carvedilol showed no difference in heart failure hospitalization or CV and all-cause mortality compared to placebo.

Digitalis does not appear to reduce heart failure hospitalizations or CV and all-cause mortality in patients with EF >45% and normal sinus rhythm. Additionally, patients 65 years and older appear more likely to be hospitalized.
Long-acting nitrate therapy was associated with worse clinical outcomes in HFPEF when compared to placebo.
Use of nebulized inorganic nitrite was also not effective in a randomized trial of 105 patients with HFpEF.
A randomized trial of sacubitril-valsartan in 4822 patients with HFpEF (EF > 45%) did not result in fewer hospitalizations or death from cardiovascular etiologies when compard to valsartan alone.

Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2i) dapagliflozin reduces hospitalization (NNT 36 over 27 months), a finding supported in a limited meta-analysis. In patients with heart failure and LVEF greater than 40%, dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily reduces the need for hospitalization due to heart failure (NNT = 36 over 2.3 years to prevent one hospitalization) but had no significant effect on mortality. At US$500 per month for 27 months at an NNT of 36, the medication cost to prevent one hospitalization is $486,000.

Adults with HFpEF, obesity and no diabetes were randomized to the GLP-1 agonist semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly SC or placebo. There were fewer serious adverse events in the semaglutide group due to significantly fewer cardiac events (2.7% vs 11.3%; P < .001; number needed to treat = 12 for 1 year) and body weight decreased by about 13.3%.
A network meta-analysis found that SGLT2i were most effective in reducing hospitalization relative to MRA and ANRi.

A 2014 Cochrane review, which included trials of patients with both HFpEF and HFrEF, concluded that exercise-based rehabilitation is associated with improved quality of life outcomes and decreased hospital admissions as compared to no exercise.A meta-analysis of five RCTs of exercise training in patients with HFpEF showed an association with improved exercise capacity, walking distance, and quality of life measures.
The importance of exercise therapy was endorsed by a AHA/ACC scientific statement (2023).

Most clinicians advise that patients with heart failure to follow a low-salt diet and to limit fluid intake, although evidence supporting this recommendation is limited. This strategy is less clearly beneficial in hospitalized patients.
Vitamin D supplementation does not improve mortality in patients with symptomatic heart failure.
Coronary revascularization is reasonable in patients with CAD if there is a clear contribution to HFpEF symptoms despite goal-directed medical treatment.

HFpEF has a similar prognosis to systolic heart failure, although the incidence of sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmias is thought to be higher in patients with HFrEF. The mortality rate at 1 year in a cohort of patients admitted to a hospital for HFpEF was 22%. Another cohort of patients hospitalized for a first episode of HFpEF showed a 5 year survival of 43% (compared to 72% for age and gender matched controls). B
The rates of readmission for heart failure and of in-hospital complications did not differ between HFpEF and HFrEF. B
The presence of ischemic heart disease and elevated levels of B-natriuretic protein adversely affects prognosis. A

A small portion of asymptomatic patients with diastolic dysfunction noted on echocardiogram will develop clinical signs of heart failure over time. One cohort study examined asymptomatic patients older than 45 with baseline echocardiography. At 6 years of followup, 2.6%, 7.8%, and 12.2% of patients with normal, mild, and moderate to severe diastolic dysfunction on echocardiography, respectively, had developed clinical heart failure.
There is an association between abdominal obesity and an increased risk of all-cause mortality (aHR 1.52, 95% CI 1.2 - 2.0) in one observational study of 3310 Japanese patients.
